claims.text: An integrated DFT, Boltzmann-transport, and ML-trained Green–Kubo method can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The integrated method will be more accurate than previous defect-free bulk models for HfNbTaTiZr.
The target HfNbTaTiZr sample is a single-phase solid solution.
The target HfNbTaTiZr sample has minimal defects and controlled oxygen content below approximately 1 wt.%.
The approach is applicable from approximately 200 K to 1200 K for chemically homogeneous, impurity-controlled HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived electronic states can provide input for calculating electronic thermal transport with a Boltzmann transport equation.
DFT will resolve the local lattice distortions of HfNbTaTiZr.
ML-trained Green–Kubo simulations can compute the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions are inherent to solid-solution high-entropy alloys.
Variation of interatomic force constants is inherent to the HfNbTaTiZr structure.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions enhance phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Enhanced phonon scattering decouples lattice thermal conductivity from electronic thermal conductivity.
Combining DFT-derived electronic states with Boltzmann transport captures the temperature evolution of electronic heat transport.
ML-trained Green–Kubo simulations capture temperature-dependent anharmonic phonon transport.
The integrated method will reduce predictive error by approximately 20–30% relative to earlier approaches.
Lattice heat transport will predominate near 200 K and become comparable to electronic heat transport at higher temperatures in HfNbTaTiZr.
Existing defect-free bulk and analytical approaches conflate lattice and electronic contributions and consequently produce less accurate predictions.
The method's accuracy will diminish for samples with substantial impurity or defect concentrations or at temperatures outside 200–1200 K.

Time-domain thermal reflectance can independently determine lattice thermal conductivity, while Hall measurements or terahertz spectroscopy can independently determine electronic thermal conductivity.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome places lattice dominance near 200 K and comparability only at higher temperatures, whereas the falsification rule calls for a crossover in dominant transport near 200 K. A crossover ordinarily denotes equality or a change in dominance, so its stated temperature is inconsistent.
